column2: So there he prayed, much-enduring godlike Odysseus,
and the strength of the mules bore the maiden to the city.
And when she came to the far-famed house of her father,
she stopped at the forecourt, and her brothers around her
stood, like the immortals, who unyoked the mules from the wagon
and carried the clothing inside.
And she went to her own chamber; and a fire was kindled for her
by the old woman from Apeire, the chamber-maid Eurymedusa,
whom once curved ships brought from Apeire;
and they picked her out as a prize for Alcinous, because he ruled over all
the Phaeacians, and the people listened to him as to a god;
she nursed white-armed Nausicaa in the halls.
She kindled the fire for her and prepared the supper inside.
And then Odysseus rose to go to the city; and Athena
poured thick mist around him, kindly disposed to Odysseus,
lest any of the great-hearted Phaeacians meeting him
mock him with words and ask him who he was.
But when he was about to enter the lovely city,
there the goddess, grey-eyed Athena, met him,
likened to a young maiden carrying a pitcher.
She stood before him, and godlike Odysseus asked her:

My child, could you not lead me to the house of the man
23	Alcinous, who rules among these people?
24	For I too, a much-tried stranger, have come here
25	from afar, from a distant land; so I know no one
26	of the men who hold this city and land.
Then again the goddess, grey-eyed Athena, said to him:

Therefore, father stranger, the house which you bid me
29	I will show you, since it dwells near my blameless father.
30	But go in silence, and I will lead the way,
31	and look at no one of men nor question any.
32	For these men do not much put up with strangers,
33	nor do they kindly love one who comes from elsewhere.
34	They, trusting in their swift ships,
35	cross the great gulf, since the Earth-shaker gave them that;
36	their ships are swift as a wing or a thought.
So speaking, Pallas Athena led the way
swiftly; and he then followed in the footsteps of the goddess.
And the ship-famed Phaeacians did not notice him
as he went through the city among them; for Athena
of the fair tresses, a dread goddess, did not allow it, and poured
a marvellous mist about him, kindly disposed in her heart.
And Odysseus wondered at the harbours and the balanced ships,
and at the assembly places of the heroes themselves and the long walls,
high, fitted with stakes, a wonder to behold.
But when they came to the far-famed house of the king,
the goddess, grey-eyed Athena, began to speak among them:

This, father stranger, is the house which you bid me
49	point out; and you will find Zeus-nurtured kings
50	feasting at dinner; but go inside, and do not fear
51	at all in your heart; for a bold man is better in all
52	deeds, even if he comes from elsewhere.
53	First you will find the mistress in the halls;
54	Arete is her name, and she is from the same
55	parents who begot king Alcinous.
56	Nausithous was first begotten by Poseidon the Earth-shaker
57	and Periboea, the best of women in form,
58	youngest daughter of great-hearted Eurymedon,
59	who once ruled over the high-spirited Giants.
60	But he destroyed his reckless people, and himself perished;
61	and Poseidon lay with her and begot a child,
62	great-hearted Nausithous, who ruled among the Phaeacians;
63	and Nausithous begot Rhexenor and Alcinous.
64	Rhexenor, though without a son, silver-bowed Apollo struck
65	as a bridegroom in his hall, leaving one only daughter,
66	Arete; and her Alcinous made his wife,
67	and honoured her as no other woman on earth is honoured,
68	of all the women who now keep house under husbands.
69	So she is honoured at heart, and has been,
70	by her dear children and by Alcinous himself
71	and by the people, who, looking on her as on a goddess,
72	greet her with words when she goes through the city.
73	For she herself is not lacking in good understanding;
74	to those for whom she thinks well she settles quarrels, even among men.
75	If she is kindly disposed to you in her heart,
76	there is hope then that you will see your friends and reach
77	your high-roofed house and your native land.
So speaking, grey-eyed Athena departed
over the unharvested sea, and left lovely Scheria,
and came to Marathon and broad-wayed Athens,
and entered the strong house of Erechtheus. And Odysseus
went to the famous house of Alcinous; and his heart much
pondered as he stood, before he reached the bronze threshold.
For there was a gleam as of the sun or the moon
through the high-roofed house of great-hearted Alcinous.
For bronze walls ran this way and that,
from the threshold to the inner part, and round them a cornice of blue enamel;
and golden doors closed the strong house within;
silver doorposts stood on the bronze threshold,
and silver lintel above, and a golden handle.
and on each side were dogs of gold and silver,
which Hephaestus made with cunning skill
to guard the house of great-hearted Alcinous,
being immortal and ageless all their days.
Inside, seats were fixed along the wall this way and that,
from the threshold to the inner part continuously, where fine robes,
well-woven, were thrown, the works of women.
There the leaders of the Phaeacians would sit
drinking and eating; for they had a constant supply.
And golden youths on well-built pedestals
stood holding blazing torches in their hands,
giving light by night through the house to the banqueters.
And fifty women servants has he in the house;
some grind the yellow grain at the mills,
and others weave webs and turn the distaffs,
sitting, like the leaves of a tall poplar;
and from the close-woven linens liquid oil drips.
As far as the Phaeacians are skilled beyond all men
in driving a swift ship on the sea, so the women
are skilled at the loom; for Athena has given them beyond others
to know very beautiful works and good wits.
Outside the court, near the doors, is a great orchard
of four acres; and a hedge runs round it on both sides.
There tall trees grow, flourishing,
pears and pomegranates and apple trees with shining fruit,
and sweet figs and flourishing olives.
Of these the fruit never perishes nor fails
in winter or in summer, all the year round; but always
the West Wind blowing makes some grow and ripens others.
Pear on pear grows old, apple on apple,
and grape-cluster on grape-cluster, and fig on fig.
There too his fruitful vineyard is rooted,
of which one part, a drying-floor on level ground,
is dried by the sun, and others they gather,
and others they tread; and in front are unripe grapes
shedding their blossom, and others beginning to darken.
There by the last row trim beds
of all kinds grow, flourishing all the year;
and in it are two springs, one of which through the whole garden
is scattered, and the other on the other side under the threshold of the court
runs to the high house, whence the townspeople drew water.
Such were the glorious gifts of the gods in the house of Alcinous.
There he stood and wondered, much-enduring godlike Odysseus.
But when he had wondered at everything in his heart,
quickly he crossed the threshold into the house.
And he found the leaders and counsellors of the Phaeacians
pouring libations with cups to the keen-sighted slayer of Argus,
to whom last they poured libations, when they thought of bed.
And he went through the house, much-enduring godlike Odysseus,
wrapped in much mist, which Athena poured about him,
until he came to Arete and to king Alcinous.
And Odysseus threw his hands about the knees of Arete,
and then the divine mist flowed away from him again.
And they fell silent throughout the house, seeing the man;
and they marvelled, looking. And Odysseus supplicated:

Arete, daughter of godlike Rhexenor,
147	to your husband and your knees I have come after much toil,
148	and to these banqueters; to them may the gods grant happy
149	lives, and may each leave to his children
150	the possessions in his halls and the honour the people gave;
151	but for me hasten an escort to reach my native land
152	sooner, since long I suffer woes far from my friends.
So saying he sat down at the hearth in the ashes
by the fire; and they all fell silent in stillness.
At last the old hero Echeneus spoke among them,
who was older than the Phaeacian men
and excelled in speech, knowing many ancient things;
he with good thought spoke out and said among them:

Alcinous, this is not fairer for you, nor is it fitting,
160	that a stranger sit on the ground at the hearth in the ashes;
161	and these men hold back, waiting for your word.
162	But come, raise the stranger up and seat him
163	on a silver-studded chair, and bid the heralds
164	to mix wine, that we may pour libations also to Zeus who delights in thunder,
165	who attends along with revered suppliants;
166	and let the housekeeper give the stranger supper from what is within.
But when the sacred might of Alcinous heard this,
taking by the hand Odysseus, shrewd of mind, of many wiles,
he raised him from the hearth and seated him on a shining chair,
having made his son rise, the brave Laodamas,
who sat next to him, and whom he loved most.
A handmaid brought water in a fair golden pitcher
and poured it over a silver basin
for him to wash; and she drew up beside him a polished table.
And the revered housekeeper brought bread and set it by,
adding many dishes, giving of what she had in store.
And he drank and ate, much-enduring godlike Odysseus.
Then the might of Alcinous said to the herald:

Pontonous, mix a bowl and distribute wine
180	to all through the hall, that we may pour libations also to Zeus who delights in thunder,
181	who attends along with revered suppliants.
So he spoke, and Pontonous mixed honey-sweet wine,
and distributed it to all, having first poured drops in the cups.
But when they had poured libations and drunk as much as their heart wished,
Alcinous spoke out and said among them:

Hear me, leaders and counsellors of the Phaeacians,
187	that I may say what the heart in my breast bids me.
188	Now, having feasted, go home and lie down;
189	and at dawn, having called more elders,
190	we shall entertain the stranger in the halls and to the gods
191	we shall offer fair sacrifices, and then also about an escort
192	we shall think, so that the stranger, without toil and distress,
193	under our escort may reach his native land
194	rejoicing quickly, even if he is from very far away,
195	and may suffer no evil or harm in between,
196	before he sets foot on his own land; and there then
197	he will suffer whatever fate and the heavy spinners
198	spun with the thread for him at his birth, when his mother bore him.
199	But if he is one of the immortals come down from heaven,
200	then this is something else the gods are contriving.
201	For always before the gods have appeared manifest
202	to us, when we perform famous hecatombs,
203	and they feast beside us, sitting just where we sit.
204	And if a lone traveller meets them on the way,
205	they do not hide at all, since we are near of kin to them,
206	as are the Cyclopes and the savage tribes of the Giants.
Answering him, Odysseus of many wiles said:

Alcinous, let some other thing be a care to your mind; for I
209	am not like the immortals, who hold the broad heaven,
210	neither in form nor in stature, but like mortal men.
211	Whomever you know to bear the most misery
212	of men, with them in sorrows I might compare myself.
213	And still more evils could I tell,
214	all that I have toiled through by the will of the gods.
215	But let me have my supper, grieved though I am;
216	for there is nothing more shameless than a hateful belly,
217	which bids a man remember it by compulsion,
218	even if he is much worn and has grief in his mind,
219	as I too have grief in my mind, yet it always
220	bids me eat and drink, and from all I have suffered
221	it makes me forget, and bids me be filled.
222	And you, make haste at the appearing of dawn,
223	that you may set me, wretched, on my native land,
224	though I have suffered much; and may life leave me, having seen
225	my property, my servants, and my great high-roofed house.
So he spoke, and they all approved and bade
send the stranger, since he had spoken as was fitting.
But when they had poured libations and drunk as much as their heart wished,
they went each to his own house to lie down,
and godlike Odysseus was left behind in the hall,
and beside him Arete and godlike Alcinous
sat; and the handmaids cleared away the dishes of the feast.
And white-armed Arete began the words among them;
for she recognized the cloak and tunic when she saw the fair
clothes, which she herself had made with her attendant women;
and speaking to him she addressed him with winged words:

Stranger, this first I myself will ask you:
238	Who are you among men, and whence? Who gave you these clothes?
239	Did you not say that you came here wandering over the sea?
Answering her, Odysseus of many wiles said:

It is hard, queen, to tell continuously
242	of my troubles, since the heavenly gods gave me many;
243	but this I will tell you, which you ask and enquire.
244	There is an island, Ogygia, lying far off in the sea;
245	there the daughter of Atlas, crafty Calypso,
246	dwells, fair-tressed, a dread goddess; and no one
247	mingles with her, neither of the gods nor of mortal men.
248	But me, unhappy, a deity brought to her hearth,
249	alone, when Zeus with a white thunderbolt struck
250	and shattered my swift ship in the midst of the wine-dark sea.
251	There all the other good companions perished,
252	but I, clasping the keel of my curved ship in my arms,
253	was carried nine days; and on the tenth black night
254	the gods brought me near to the island of Ogygia, where Calypso
255	dwells, fair-tressed, a dread goddess, who took me in
256	and kindly loved me and nurtured me, and said that she would
257	make me immortal and ageless all my days;
258	but she never persuaded my heart in my breast.
259	There I stayed seven years continuously, and the clothes
260	I always wet with tears, which Calypso gave me, immortal ones;
261	but when the eighth year came round for me,
262	then she bade me go, urging me,
263	either by a message from Zeus, or her own mind was turned.
264	She sent me on a raft of many bindings, and gave me many things,
265	bread and sweet wine, and clothed me in immortal clothes,
266	and sent a wind, harmless and gentle.
267	Seventeen days I sailed, voyaging over the sea,
268	and on the eighteenth the shadowy mountains appeared
269	of your land, and my dear heart rejoiced,
270	unlucky me; for I was still to meet with misery
271	great, which Poseidon the Earth-shaker raised against me,
272	who, rushing the winds upon me, bound my way,
273	and stirred the sea immeasurably, nor did the wave
274	allow the raft, groaning thickly, to be carried on.
275	That then the storm scattered; but I myself
276	swimming cut across this gulf, until wind and water,
277	carrying me, brought me near your land.
278	There, as I came out, a wave would have forced me onto the shore,
279	dashing me against great rocks and a joyless place;
280	but drawing back I swam again, until I came
281	to a river, where the place seemed best to me,
282	smooth of rocks, and there was shelter from the wind.
283	I fell out, recovering my spirit, and ambrosial night
284	came on. And I, going apart from the Zeus-fallen river,
285	slept in the bushes, and heaped leaves about me;
286	and a god poured boundless sleep upon me.
287	There among the leaves, grieved in my dear heart,
288	I slept all night and into the dawn and the mid-day.
289	The sun declined, and sweet sleep released me.
290	And I noticed the handmaids of your daughter on the shore
291	playing, and she herself was among them, like the goddesses;
292	her I supplicated; and she did not fail in good understanding,
293	such as you would not expect a younger person meeting you
294	to show; for always the younger are foolish.
295	She gave me bread in plenty and sparkling wine,
296	and had me bathe in the river, and gave me these clothes.
297	This I have told you truly, grieved though I am.
Then Alcinous answered him and spoke:

Stranger, indeed in this my child did not
300	think rightly, that she did not bring you with her
301	handmaids to our house, though you supplicated her first.
Answering him, Odysseus of many wiles said:
Then Alcinous answered him and spoke:

Stranger, my heart in my breast is not such
310	as to be angered idly; better is all that is right.
311	Would that, father Zeus and Athena and Apollo,
312	being such as you are, and thinking what I think,
313	you might have my daughter and be called my son-in-law,
314	staying here; a house and possessions I would give,
315	if you stayed willingly; but against your will no one
316	of the Phaeacians will hold you; let this not be dear to father Zeus.
317	And for an escort I appoint this time, that you may know well:
318	tomorrow; then you, overcome by sleep,
319	will lie down, and they will row over the calm, until you reach
320	your native land and house, and wherever is dear to you,
321	even if it is much farther than Euboea,
322	which they say is the farthest, those of our people
323	who saw it, when they took fair-haired Rhadamanthys
324	to visit Tityus, son of Earth.
325	And they went there and accomplished it without toil
326	on the same day, and finished it back home.
327	And you will know in your own mind how much the best
328	are my ships and my youths at tossing the sea with the oar-blade.
So he spoke, and much-enduring godlike Odysseus rejoiced,
and praying he spoke, and spoke a word and called him by name:
So they spoke such things to one another;
and white-armed Arete ordered her handmaids
to place beds under the portico and to throw on fair
purple blankets, and to spread rugs over them
and to put woollen cloaks on top to be covered with.
And they went out of the hall holding torches in their hands;
and when they had spread the thick bed, hurrying,
they urged Odysseus, standing beside him with words:
Rise to sleep, stranger; your bed has been made.
So they spoke, and sleeping seemed welcome to him.
So there he slept, much-enduring godlike Odysseus,
on a corded bedstead under the echoing portico;
and Alcinous lay down in the inner part of the high house,
and beside him his wife, the lady, prepared bed and couch.
